title: Joshua 22:21–34
context: The eastern tribes explain that the altar is a witness, not a place of sacrifice, meant to keep their children from being cut off from the LORD. Phinehas accepts their answer, Israel blesses God, and war is averted.

verses.text: Then the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh answered, and spoke to the heads of the thousands of Israel,
verses.arminianNotes: The eastern tribes answer the heads of Israel. Arminian readers see them given the chance to speak, which the narrative presents as essential to resolving the conflict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a response offered before judgment is carried out. The verse introduces their defense, which will clarify their intention.

verses.text: “The Mighty One, God, the LORD, the Mighty One, God, the LORD, he knows; and Israel shall know: if it was in rebellion, or if in trespass against the LORD (don’t save us today),
verses.arminianNotes: They cry, “The Mighty One, God, the LORD … he knows; and Israel shall know.” Arminian readers see an appeal to God’s knowledge of their hearts, offered with deep sincerity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God invoked as witness to their motives. The repetition of the divine names expresses urgency and solemnity in their oath.

verses.text: that we have built us an altar to turn away from following the LORD; or if to offer burnt offering or meal offering, or if to offer sacrifices of peace offerings, let the LORD himself require it.
verses.arminianNotes: They say that if they built the altar for sacrifice, “let the LORD himself require it.” Arminian readers see willingness to accept God’s judgment if they have done wrong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the tribes submitting their case to God. Their words show that they share the concern for the single altar of the LORD.

verses.text: “If we have not out of concern done this, and for a reason, saying, ‘In time to come your children might speak to our children, saying, “What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: They explain they acted out of concern that future children might say, “What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?” Arminian readers see worry about future exclusion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a desire to preserve covenant identity across generations. The tribes reveal a motive rooted in faithfulness rather than rebellion.

verses.text: For the LORD has made the Jordan a border between us and you, you children of Reuben and children of Gad. You have no portion in the LORD.” ’ So your children might make our children cease from fearing the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: They fear the Jordan will become a border and their children told, “You have no portion in the LORD.” Arminian readers see concern that geography could weaken faith over time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a fear that future generations might be separated from the worship of Israel. Their concern is for the next generation’s fear of the LORD.

verses.text: “Therefore we said, ‘Let’s now prepare to build ourselves an altar, not for burnt offering, nor for sacrifice;
verses.arminianNotes: They say, “Let’s now prepare to build ourselves an altar, not for burnt offering, nor for sacrifice.” Arminian readers see a carefully explained purpose that avoids rivaling the true altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the distinction between a memorial and a place of sacrifice. The verse begins to clarify that the altar was never meant for offerings.

verses.text: but it will be a witness between us and you, and between our generations after us, that we may perform the service of the LORD before him with our burnt offerings, with our sacrifices, and with our peace offerings;’ that your children may not tell our children in time to come, ‘You have no portion in the LORD.’
verses.arminianNotes: The altar is a witness so they may serve the LORD and so future children may not say, “You have no portion in the LORD.” Arminian readers see a memorial meant to safeguard unity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the altar functioning as testimony rather than worship. Its purpose is to preserve the eastern tribes’ access to the LORD’s sanctuary across generations.

verses.text: “Therefore we said, ‘It shall be, when they tell us or our generations this in time to come, that we shall say, “Behold the pattern of the LORD’s altar, which our fathers made, not for burnt offering, nor for sacrifice; but it is a witness between us and you.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: They explain they would say, “Behold the pattern of the LORD’s altar … it is a witness between us and you.” Arminian readers see a copy that points back to the true altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the altar’s design as a reminder of the one sanctuary. The explanation removes the charge of rival worship.

verses.text: “Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD, and turn away today from following the LORD, to build an altar for burnt offering, for meal offering, or for sacrifice, besides the LORD our God’s altar that is before his tabernacle!”
verses.arminianNotes: They say, “Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD.” Arminian readers see a sincere denial of apostasy and a commitment to the one altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a clear confession of loyalty to the LORD’s altar before his tabernacle. Their words echo the delegation’s concern and resolve it.

verses.text: When Phinehas the priest, and the princes of the congregation, even the heads of the thousands of Israel that were with him, heard the words that the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the children of Manasseh spoke, it pleased them well.
verses.arminianNotes: Phinehas and the leaders hear the explanation and are pleased. Arminian readers see conflict resolved through honest speech and careful listening.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the leaders accepting a credible account. The verse marks the turning point from accusation to reconciliation.

verses.text: Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest said to the children of Reuben, to the children of Gad, and to the children of Manasseh, “Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this trespass against the LORD. Now you have delivered the children of Israel out of the LORD’s hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: Phinehas says, “Today we know that the LORD is among us.” Arminian readers see relief that the community remains faithful and that judgment has been averted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s presence affirmed through the absence of trespass. Phinehas recognizes that the eastern tribes have spared Israel from the danger of divine judgment.

verses.text: Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, and the princes, returned from the children of Reuben, and from the children of Gad, out of the land of Gilead, to the land of Canaan, to the children of Israel, and brought them word again.
verses.arminianNotes: Phinehas and the princes return to Canaan and report. Arminian readers see the delegation completing its task with a peaceful outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the matter brought back to the whole community. The verse ensures that the resolution is shared publicly with Israel.

verses.text: The thing pleased the children of Israel; and the children of Israel blessed God, and spoke no more of going up against them to war, to destroy the land in which the children of Reuben and the children of Gad lived.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel is pleased, blesses God, and abandons plans for war. Arminian readers see gratitude and peace replacing suspicion, a model for resolving disputes among God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see praise offered to God for the peaceful outcome. The verse shows how careful inquiry prevented unnecessary bloodshed.

verses.text: The children of Reuben and the children of Gad named the altar “A Witness Between Us that the LORD is God.”
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben and Gad name the altar “A Witness Between Us that the LORD is God.” Arminian readers see a lasting reminder of shared faith and the danger of hasty judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the altar’s name confessing the LORD as God. The chapter ends with unity restored around a common confession, without forcing a doctrinal dispute onto the narrative.
